holidays.name: National Daiquiri Day
holidays.description: A toast to the frosty, rum-based cocktail that has been cooling off sunburned sippers for over a century. Whether you like yours classic with lime or blended with strawberries, today is the day to raise a glass.
holidays.origin: The daiquiri is traditionally credited to American mining engineer Jennings Cox, who supposedly created it around 1900 in the Cuban town of Daiquirí when he ran out of gin. The unofficial holiday grew out of American cocktail-calendar culture.
holidays.funFact: President John F. Kennedy was a famous fan of daiquiris, and the drink became popular in Washington after the cocktail was reportedly served on Navy ships and at diplomatic events.

holidays.name: National Raspberry Cake Day
holidays.description: A day for baking, slicing, and devouring cakes studded with tart, jewel-like raspberries. Layer it, frost it, or swirl it into cream cheese, but make sure the berries get their moment in the spotlight.
holidays.origin: Like many food observances, this one emerged from the unofficial American food-holiday calendar, spread by bakers and food bloggers who wanted a summery excuse to celebrate berry season.
holidays.funFact: Raspberries are not true berries in the botanical sense. They are aggregate fruits made of many tiny drupelets, each with its own seed.

holidays.name: Flip Flop Day
holidays.description: A day to celebrate the humble thong sandal, the footwear of beaches, pool decks, and questionable office casual Fridays. Strap on your flip-flops and let your toes breathe in all their glory.
holidays.origin: Flip-flops trace back thousands of years to ancient Egypt, and the modern rubber version became wildly popular in the United States after soldiers returning from Japan after World War II brought home zori sandals. The day is an informal summer observance.
holidays.funFact: The name flip-flop comes from the sound the sandals make when you walk in them.

holidays.name: Stick Out Your Tongue Day
holidays.description: An entire day dedicated to being cheeky by sticking your tongue out at friends, family, and the camera. It is the perfect excuse to be silly and shed your serious face.
holidays.origin: Often tied to the famous 1951 photograph of Albert Einstein sticking out his tongue, which was taken on his 72nd birthday. The informal observance has spread online as a playful tribute to goofiness.
holidays.funFact: Einstein reportedly stuck his tongue out at a photographer who asked him to smile one more time, and he liked the photo so much that he ordered copies to send to friends.

holidays.name: Get to Know Your Customers Day
holidays.description: A business-flavored quirky holiday that encourages companies to step out from behind the spreadsheet and actually talk to the people who buy their stuff. Surveys, chats, and genuine curiosity are all welcome.
holidays.origin: Created by customer service consultant Jeff Mowatt in 2012, it is observed on the third Thursday of each quarter, though it is often listed on calendars on various dates by businesses and trade groups.
holidays.funFact: Studies often cited in business circles suggest that acquiring a new customer can cost several times more than keeping an existing one, which is why this day is about listening, not just selling.
